blocks.text: Capacitors are used in many household appliances, such as electric fans, water pumps, washing machines, refrigerators, flashguns, computer keyboards and touchscreens.

A capacitor is connected to the starting circuit of a fan motor (Fig 16.17). When the power is switched on, the capacitor helps the motor overcome static friction and the inertia of the rotor so that it starts and begins spinning quickly. Capacitors play the same role in the motors of washing machines, blenders, choppers, grinders and water pumps.

The compressors of refrigerators and air conditioners usually use single-phase motors, which can struggle to start on their own, so capacitors of high capacitance are used. Such a 'start capacitor' acts like a jump start for the compressor motor, getting it rotating; once the motor reaches a certain speed, a relay disconnects it. Most refrigerators and air conditioners also have a 'run capacitor' that stays connected to improve energy efficiency, though some older models use only start capacitors. Capacitors with resistors also form time-delay circuits, used in refrigerators, air conditioners and other devices to delay switching on the power, which protects them from power fluctuations (Fig 16.18, a photograph of a compressor, is not reproduced).

In a flashgun, a capacitor stores and releases electrical energy to power the flash tube, which contains xenon gas. The capacitor is charged from the camera's battery. When the shutter button is pressed, the capacitor is connected to the flash tube, and its rapid discharge provides the high current needed to ionise the xenon, which gives a burst of bright light (Fig 16.19 is a photograph of a camera).

Capacitors are widely used in rectification, converting alternating current (AC) into direct current (DC); a full-wave rectifier called a bridge circuit is a typical example, and rectifiers are studied in the next chapter. In medicine, capacitors store the electrical energy needed to deliver a life-saving shock to the heart to restore a normal rhythm after cardiac arrest (a defibrillator). They are also used in imaging machines (CT, MRI, X-ray, ultrasound) to filter out noise and improve image clarity, and they filter out unwanted signals in EEG and ECG machines.

Top right: a flashgun circuit in which a battery charges a capacitor that is switched across a xenon tube. Bottom right: rectified pulses (blue, dashed) and the much steadier voltage with a smoothing capacitor (red).
blocks.caption: Some uses of capacitors (original diagram after Figs 16.17 to 16.19).
blocks.long_description: In each device the capacitor either stores charge and releases it quickly (flash, defibrillator), shifts the timing of a current (motor), or fills in the gaps between pulses (rectifier).
